extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiner practices to explicitly document how claim language is being interpreted (BRI, §112(f), optional/functional language, printed matter, etc.) on the record during patent prosecution. Aims to improve clarity for applicants, the public, and later review by courts/PTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documenting claim scope during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: More thoroughly document key issues of claim scope during prosecution; explicitly inform patent owner and public of the decision making during prosecution; clearly record the examiner’s reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record on the file why claims are interpreted as they are so applicants and the public understand examiner reasoning and to avoid prosecution delays due to misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: During patent examination, claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art; the BRI of the claim is then used to evaluate patentability under each of the statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish the BRI clearly on the record and use that BRI when examining claims for patentability (e.g., in anticipation/obviousness rejections). The Pilot addresses putting the BRI and the examiner’s understanding on the record for certain claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and identify special definitions of claim terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Under BRI, words of a claim are given their plain meaning unless inconsistent with the specification. Applicants can rebut the plain meaning by clearly setting forth a special definition of the term in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a special definition is used, identify the claim term and the special definition and note where it appears in the specification so the record shows the claim was interpreted using the special definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify language that suggests optional limitations and explain whether limiting
rubrics_metrics.description: Language that suggests or makes optional, but does not require, a particular structure or particular steps to be performed does not limit the claim scope. Examples include “adapted to/for” clauses, “for example” phrases, “such as” phrases, “wherein” clauses, and “whereby” clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify such optional language on the record and explain whether it has a limiting effect on claim scope; determination depends on particular facts, so explain the factual basis for whether it limits BRI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate functional language and note §112(f) implications
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation is functional when it recites a feature by what it does rather than by what it is. The BRI will depend on whether §112(f) (means-plus-function) is invoked or not. When §112(f) is not invoked, whether the BRI is limited by the function turns on the existence of a connection between the functional language and structure, material, or acts recited in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether functional language limits the BRI of the claim and explain why. In the Pilot, when functional language is present without invoking §112(f), add a statement whether it has been given patentable weight along with explanation and examples (e.g., 'function Y limits the operation of widget A' vs 'function Y is unconnected to any structure... and therefore imposes no limits').

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify statements of intended use, purpose, or result and indicate limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of intended use or result typically does not provide a patentable distinction unless some structural or manipulative difference is imposed on the claimed structure or action; intended use/result can appear in a preamble or claim body and is evaluated case-by-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify statements of intended use/purpose/result and indicate whether they impose any limits on the BRI. Pay particular attention to preambles and whether they limit claim scope; record the rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether non-functional descriptive material (printed matter) is given patentable weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-functional descriptive material (printed matter) refers to content of information recited in a claim (e.g., dosage instructions on a label). As claims are read as a whole, printed matter may not be disregarded, but absent a new and unobvious functional relationship between the material and the substrate patentable weight need not be given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify descriptive material in the claim, explain whether a functional relationship is found between the material and the product or step claimed, and state whether the material is being given patentable weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply §112(f) (means-plus-function) presumptions and explain when overcome
rubrics_metrics.description: When functional language is used in a claim, determine whether §112(f) is being invoked. Use of the word “means” raises a rebuttable presumption that §112(f) applies; absence of the word “means” raises a rebuttable presumption that §112(f) does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note the §112(f) presumptions on the record and explain when they have been overcome. Specifically identify language using 'means' or generic placeholders and explain why §112(f) is or is not invoked, using FP 7.30.04 when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: When §112(f) is invoked, identify corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation is to be treated under §112(f), corresponding structure, material, or acts in the specification must be identified as performing the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a best practice, identify the corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification on the record to clearly establish the BRI for that claim limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: For computer-implemented functions, classify specialized vs non-specialized and identify algorithms/hardware when required
rubrics_metrics.description: Programmed computer functions that invoke §112(f) require a computer programmed with an 'algorithm' to perform the function and fall into specialized (requiring 'special programming' and disclosure of algorithm) and non-specialized (commonly performed by a general purpose computer) types. It is rare that an algorithm need not be disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Pilot, identify programmed computer functions that invoke §112(f) and indicate whether: (a) the function is non-specialized and can be achieved by any general purpose computer without special programming, or (b) the function is specialized and is performed with hardware and algorithm identified in the specification. Describe the hardware and algorithm or indicate where they appear in the specification. For non-specialized functions, best practice is to identify the algorithm in the specification to establish the BRI, and explain if asserting that disclosure is not required (a rare circumstance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the established claim interpretation in rejections and explain how it affects patentability analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the BRI is clearly established and explanations for the types of language focused on in this Pilot are on the record, use that BRI and explanation when examining the claims for patentability under the statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making rejections (e.g., anticipation), explicitly tie the rejection to the claim interpretation on the record—for example, noting that an intended use is not given weight because it does not impose a limit on claim scope as explained in the claim construction portion of the Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage Pilot results to determine best practices and evaluate benefits vs resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the results of the Pilot to determine examiner-identified enhanced clarity practices and evaluate benefits versus resources and how explanations assist in articulating prior art rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect examples of examiner-identified enhanced clarity practices, assess resource impacts, and evaluate whether the recorded explanations materially assist clarity of prior art rejections and prosecution outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a clear record to enable applicant response and downstream use by courts/PTAB and public
rubrics_metrics.description: By providing enhanced claim interpretation on the record, the Pilot aims to provide an opportunity for applicants to agree or respond to the examiner’s claim interpretation, provide information for courts and the PTAB, provide certainty as to the boundaries of the claims, and enable potential users to make informed decisions concerning scope of issued patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the record includes sufficient explanation of interpretation choices (special definitions, non-weighted terms, §112(f) invocation, algorithm/hardware identification) so applicants, courts, PTAB, and public can understand and act on the examiner’s interpretation.
